I want to pull back to minimum platform support in
our testing. This will potentially make users adopt
our versions of compilers, but it makes our lives
much much easier.

The constraints from R come from its default Makeconf

R:
g++ -O2 (default)
g++ -O3 (our reco upgrade)

and lead to the constraints:

Mac:
g++ latest XCode with -O0, -O2, -O3, default flags
==> 4.2.1

Windows
g++ latest RTools with default flags and -O2 and -03
==> 4.6.3

Linux
g++ latest stable version, with default flags and -O0, -O2, -O3
==> ???

I would like to support clang++, because it's what we're also using:

Mac
clang++ latest Xcode with -O0, -O2, -O3, default flags
==> 3.1

Linux
clang++ latest stable version, with default flags and -O0, -O2, -O3
==> ???


If we support the above, I feel OK leaving everything else to
our users to test.

Ben -- what's the "canonical" Linux version of g++ and clang++?
And do our tests pass on them?

Our tests all pass on Mac and Windows with the above configs.

- Bob

our users to test.

Ben -- what's the "canonical" Linux version of g++ and clang++?
And do our tests pass on them?

There isn't a "canonical" Linux anything. The most widely used personal variants are in the Ubuntu family but the toolchain varies depending on what version you are using. The most widely used server variants are in the Red Hat family, where again the toolchain varies but tends to be older than what an individual would have.

With the current Stan makefile, CC=g++ by default. On a Linux system, g++ is usually a symlink to some versioned g++ like g++-4.6. We have no way of knowing what g++ points to. I would say the expectation of the community is that any program should work with the latest stable upstream version of a compiler, which is g++-4.7.x currently (4.8 is a few months off). But the expectation of the community is that any program should typically work with some older versions of the compiler, unless there is a compelling reason why that is impossible, because Linux distributions (particularly for servers) default to compilers that were released a few years ago. For example, our own Hotfoot scientific computing servers (RHEL) have this software

https://wikis.cuit.columbia.edu/confluence/display/rcs/Hotfoot+Software

e.g. gcc-4.1 is the default but gcc-4.4 is available. That is a bit extreme but not atypical for a server.

Ben

Agreed.  Basically two tiers of supported platforms:

1) Tested to work, we run test-unit and don't release if it breaks.  This is a small number of specific configurations based on what gives us good coverage and what we can manage.
2) Ideally should work.  I.E., generic combinations of platforms/compilers/optimization levels/etc.  For instance we could simply say any platform supported by both Eigen and Boost should work.  Or any platform with versions of gcc >= 4.4 or clang++ >= 3.0.  This is the largest pool of configurations and ideally developers occasionally touch some on them occasionally.


Some projects handle this by leading with 2) and then following with 1).  For instance,

"Stan should work on any platform and compiler which is supported by both Eigen and Boost and has been known to work on the following system configurations <list from 2>.  Failure to work on these, or any other Eigen and Boost supported platform should be reported as a bug.  Stan is routinely tested and should always work under the following configurations: <list from 1>"

On Friday, December 14, 2012 6:33:59 PM UTC-5, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
Agreed.  Basically two tiers of supported platforms:

Yes. When I created the wiki page, I wasn't intending it to define the tiers of support, which I think is more appropriate for the manual or for mc-stan.org. I just called it "Results of test-unit for various configurations" so that we could list as many working or not working configurations that have been tested at a particular SHA. Also to have a central place where the current error messages were listed so we wouldn't have to dig through the list.

But the wiki page is something completely different now, doesn't convey Marcus' principles, doesn't make that much sense. If we say, "here are the configurations that we wouldn't release Stan without passing test-unit", then do we really need to say "and here are the SHAs where they, in fact, passed"? Users can assume test-unit passage for those configurations at any v1.0.x tag, and users shouldn't really care if those configurations happen to be temporarily broken at any intermediate commit.

The other thing that bothers me is that if we generally expect Stan to work in situations where Boost and Eigen generally work, and we find a configuration where that is not the case, we should presume it is a Stan bug, instead of saying we don't care unless it is a Tier I supported configuration. If we can conclusively say it is an Eigen bug, a Boost bug, a compiler bug, etc. and report it upstream and they acknowledge it, that is fine and we can document that Stan will not work in that situation for reasons that are out of our control. But for something like the current situation with clang-3.2 yielding weird Boost warnings and parser failures, we do not yet know where the bug is yet. That isn't necessarily a reason to hold up v1.0.4, but we should be actively trying to work on it because it could imply that the Stan code is silently doing the wrong or suboptimal thing in "working" configurations.

For stanc in particular, our tests don't really tell us whether we are generating the expected C++ code or whether it is compiling in the expected way. We just know if a .stan file parses or not. The test-models target helps a little bit here, but it is sort of blunt and we aren't paying too much attention when some model is reported to fail.

Ben

One possibility that occurred to me after sleeping on it
is that some of the subgrammars might not be getting
initialized properly. This would lead to the same kind of
behavior that Daniel was talking about when things weren't getting
built properly in Windows due to size problems.

Could someone do a sanity check on the way I coded the grammars
I describe below.

(Another check would be to test whether the grammars worked before
I added the subgrammar business for comparison and boolean ops and
if-then and while statements.)

The last thing I had to do to shrink the size of the individual
translation units for statements and expressions was to doubly
link the structures involved in the recursive grammars.

The grammar looks like this from 10,000 feet:

A1 -> A2 -> ... -> AM -> ... -> AN -> A1

In practice, say A1 is an expression with addition operators,
A2 the rule for multiplicative operators, etc., down to basic
expressions AN, which include parenthesized expressions of
precedence A1.

So I created two grammars, one for A1, and one cut in the middle
for AM, and had the A1 grammar construct the AM grammar by
passing a self-pointer as a reference. Here are the relevant
code snippets.

Techical grammar aside: the "allow_lte" flag in the ctor
indicates where to start in the expression tree in order to resolve
the ambiguity the parser sees in evaluating the final

int<lower = 0> x;
int< lower = 0>b > x;

The second form is illegal and its intent must be expressed as

real<lower = (0 > b)> x;

Actually, it's looking for "*/" if it sees an opening
comment. So the first thing in the file is going to
be a "/*" open comment, and I'm guessing it somehow mangles
the middle and never finds the closing "*/".

>
> |
> goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/opt/stan$ grep -A 1 "requested here\|warning: returning" /tmp/clang_warnings.txt
> lib/boost_1.52.0/boost/iterator/iterator_adaptor.hpp:306:18: warning: returning reference to local temporary object
> [-Wreturn-stack-address]
> { return *m_iterator; }
> --
> boost::forward_traversal_tag, boost::use_default, boost::use_default>::dereference' requested here
> return f.dereference();

This is where it's trying to do the buffering -- this is
all encoded in forward-type iterators, which are then wrapped
in buffering iterators.

...

> --
> boost::spirit::char_encoding::ascii> >, 0> &>, 2> >' requested here
> = ( omit["/*"] >> *(char_ - "*/") > omit["*/"] ) ###
> --

This rule's ignoring any further "/*" because they don't nest, then
looking for a sequence of chars, stopping before it finds a "*/"
--- that's the *(char_ - "*/") part. Then it just jumps over
the last "*/" using "omit".

The point is that there's lots of implicit lookahead every time you consume
a char within a comment to make sure it's not followed by a "*/".

...

> lib/boost_1.52.0/boost/iterator/iterator_adaptor.hpp:306:18: warning: returning reference to local temporary object
> [-Wreturn-stack-address]
> { return *m_iterator; }

I don't know if this warning is benign or not. This
is partly why I'm worried about the fact that the
C++11 standard changed the internal type returns inside
the base iterator type we're using:

std::istreambuf_iterator<char>

Here's the link again, indicating changed behavior as of g++ 4.7:

http://gcc.gnu.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=50336

http://gcc.1065356.n5.nabble.com/Bug-libstdc-50336-New-LWG-issue-445-td347525.html

> > >::************>::failed' requested here
> BOOST_CONCEPT_USAGE(InputIterator)

This is a new thing in Boost 1.52 that checks if a type
implements the appropriate set of concepts to be used
to instantiate a type. I believe if it doesn't, Boost
relies on the substitution failure is not an error (SFINAE)
pattern, which is why you'd see something like the above.

So anotehr possibility would be to back off to Boost 1.51
and see if that's working with the parser.
